1: The Way that can be told is not the constant Way; the name that can be named is not the constant name. Nameless, it is the beginning of heaven and earth; named, it is the mother of the ten thousand things. So, ever without desire, one sees its subtlety; ever with desire, one sees where it ends. These two come out together but are named differently; together they are called the dark. Dark upon dark: the gate of all subtleties.
2: When all under heaven know beauty as beauty, there is already ugliness; when all know good as good, there is already the not-good. So being and non-being give birth to each other, hard and easy complete each other, long and short measure each other, high and low lean on each other, note and voice harmonize with each other, front and back follow each other. Therefore the sage abides in doing without contrivance and practices the teaching without words. The ten thousand things arise and he does not turn them away; he gives them life but does not possess them, acts but does not rely on it, completes the work but does not dwell in it. Because he does not dwell in it, it never leaves him.
3: Do not exalt the worthy, and the people will not contend. Do not prize goods hard to get, and the people will not steal. Do not display what can be desired, and the people's hearts will not be stirred. So the sage governs by emptying their hearts and filling their bellies, softening their ambitions and strengthening their bones. He keeps the people without cunning and without craving, and sees that the clever do not dare to act. Act without contrivance, and nothing will be left ungoverned.
4: The Way is empty, yet in use it is never filled; deep, it seems the ancestor of the ten thousand things. It blunts the sharp, unties the tangled, softens the glare, and mingles with the dust. Still and clear, it seems perhaps to be there. I do not know whose child it is; it seems to come before the Lord on High.
5: Heaven and earth are not humane; they treat the ten thousand things as straw dogs. The sage is not humane; he treats the people as straw dogs. The space between heaven and earth, is it not like a bellows? Empty, yet never exhausted; the more it moves, the more comes out. Many words soon run out; better to keep to the center.
6: The spirit of the valley never dies; it is called the dark female. The gate of the dark female is called the root of heaven and earth. Unbroken, as if always there; use it, and it never wears out.
7: Heaven endures and earth lasts. Heaven and earth can endure and last because they do not live for themselves; so they live long. Therefore the sage puts himself last and finds himself first, treats himself as outside and finds himself preserved. Is it not because he has no self-interest? So he can fulfill himself.
8: The highest good is like water. Water benefits the ten thousand things and does not contend; it stays in the places people dislike, and so it is close to the Way. In dwelling, good is the ground; in the heart, good is depth; in giving, good is kindness; in speech, good is trust; in governing, good is order; in affairs, good is ability; in action, good is timing. Because it does not contend, it incurs no blame.
9: To hold a thing and fill it to the brim is not as good as stopping in time. Hammer an edge to sharpness and it cannot keep for long. A hall full of gold and jade, no one can guard it; wealth and rank with arrogance bring their own ruin. When the work is done, step back: that is the Way of heaven.
10: Carrying the soul and embracing the One, can you keep them from parting? Concentrating your breath to reach softness, can you be like an infant? Cleansing the dark mirror, can you leave no flaw? Loving the people and governing the state, can you do without cunning? As heaven's gate opens and closes, can you play the female? Clear and bright in every direction, can you do without contrivance? It gives life and rears them; gives life but does not possess, acts but does not rely on it, raises them but does not rule them. This is called dark virtue.
11: Thirty spokes share one hub; it is the empty space that makes the cart useful. Clay is shaped into a vessel; it is the empty space that makes the vessel useful. Doors and windows are cut to make a room; it is the empty space that makes the room useful. So what is there gives the benefit, and what is not there gives the use.
12: The five colors blind the eye, the five notes deafen the ear, the five flavors dull the palate; racing and hunting madden the heart, and goods hard to get hinder one's conduct. Therefore the sage cares for the belly, not the eye. So he rejects that and takes this.
13: Favor and disgrace alike are alarming; prize great trouble as you prize your body. What does it mean that favor and disgrace alike are alarming? Favor is lowly: gaining it is alarming, losing it is alarming. That is what it means. What does it mean to prize great trouble as your body? The reason I have great trouble is that I have a body; if I had no body, what trouble would I have? So one who prizes his own person as he would the world can be entrusted with the world; one who loves his own person as he would the world can be given the world in trust.
14: Looked at but not seen, it is called the invisible; listened to but not heard, it is called the inaudible; grasped at but not caught, it is called the intangible. These three cannot be fathomed, so they blend into one. Its top is not bright, its bottom not dark; unending, it cannot be named, and it returns again to nothing. This is the shape without shape, the image without a thing; it is called the elusive and evasive. Meet it and you do not see its head; follow it and you do not see its back. Hold to the Way of old to manage what exists today. To know the ancient beginning is called the thread of the Way.
15: Those of old who were good at being officers were subtle, mysterious, profound, and penetrating, too deep to be known. Because they cannot be known, I can only describe them by force: hesitant, as if crossing a river in winter; wary, as if fearing neighbors on all sides; dignified, like a guest; yielding, like ice about to melt; simple, like uncarved wood; open, like a valley; murky, like muddy water. Who can make the muddy still and slowly clear? Who can make the calm move for long and slowly come to life? Those who keep this Way do not wish to be full. Because they are not full, they can stay worn and not be newly made.
16: Reach the utmost emptiness; hold fast to stillness. The ten thousand things rise together, and I watch them return. Things flourish in abundance, and each returns to its root. Returning to the root is called stillness; this is called returning to one's destiny. Returning to destiny is called the constant; knowing the constant is called clarity. Not knowing the constant, one acts recklessly and meets misfortune. Knowing the constant, one is all-embracing; all-embracing, one is impartial; impartial, one is kingly; kingly, one is like heaven; like heaven, one is with the Way; with the Way, one endures, and to the end of life one is in no danger.
17: The best rulers: those below merely know they exist. Next: they are loved and praised. Next: they are feared. Next: they are despised. When trust is lacking, there is distrust. Unhurried, the best ruler values his words. The work is done, the task achieved, and the people all say, "We did it naturally ourselves."
18: When the great Way is abandoned, there are humaneness and righteousness. When cleverness and knowledge appear, there is great falseness. When the six relations are out of harmony, there are filial piety and parental love. When the state is in disorder, there are loyal ministers.
19: Cut off sageliness, discard knowledge, and the people will benefit a hundredfold. Cut off humaneness, discard righteousness, and the people will return to filial piety and love. Cut off craft, discard profit, and there will be no thieves. These three, taken as ornament, are not enough; so let people have something to hold to: show plainness, embrace the uncarved, lessen self-interest, reduce desires.
20: Cut off learning and there will be no worries. Between a yes and a yeah, how much difference is there? Between good and bad, how far apart are they? What others fear, one cannot but fear. How vast, with no end in sight! The crowd is merry, as if feasting at a great sacrifice, as if climbing a terrace in spring. I alone am placid, giving no sign, like an infant who has not yet learned to smile; listless, as if with nowhere to return. The crowd all have more than enough, and I alone seem to have lost out. Mine is the heart of a fool! Muddled and dull. Ordinary people are bright; I alone am dim. Ordinary people are sharp; I alone am dull. Calm like the sea, drifting as if without rest. The crowd all have their uses; I alone am stubborn and rustic. I alone differ from others, and I prize being fed by the mother.
21: The bearing of great virtue follows the Way alone. The Way as a thing is elusive and evasive. Evasive and elusive, yet within it there is an image; elusive and evasive, yet within it there is a thing. Dim and dark, yet within it there is an essence; that essence is utterly real, and within it there is trust. From of old until now its name has never gone, and by it we see the beginning of all things. How do I know what the beginning of all things is like? By this.
22: Bent, then whole; crooked, then straight; hollow, then full; worn, then new; little, then gain; much, then confusion. Therefore the sage embraces the One and becomes the model for the world. He does not show himself, so he is seen clearly; he does not insist he is right, so he is recognized; he does not boast, so he has merit; he does not brag, so he lasts. Because he does not contend, no one in the world can contend with him. What the ancients said, "Bent, then whole," was it an empty saying? Truly, wholeness returns to him.
23: To speak little is natural. So a whirlwind does not last the morning, a downpour does not last the day. Who makes these? Heaven and earth. If even heaven and earth cannot keep them going long, how much less can man? So one who follows the Way in his affairs: with those of the Way, he is one with the Way; with those of virtue, one with virtue; with those who have lost, one with loss. One with the Way, the Way gladly receives him; one with virtue, virtue gladly receives him; one with loss, loss gladly receives him. When trust is lacking, there is distrust.
24: On tiptoe, one cannot stand; with straddling strides, one cannot walk. One who shows himself is not seen clearly; one who insists he is right is not recognized; one who boasts has no merit; one who brags does not last. In the light of the Way, these are called leftover food and useless growths. Things may detest them, so one who has the Way does not dwell in them.
25: There was a thing formed in chaos, born before heaven and earth. Silent and empty, standing alone and unchanging, going round everywhere without danger, it can be the mother of the world. I do not know its name; I style it "the Way," and forced to name it, I call it "great." Great means going on; going on means far away; far away means turning back. So the Way is great, heaven is great, earth is great, and the king too is great. Within the realm there are four great ones, and the king is one of them. Man follows earth, earth follows heaven, heaven follows the Way, and the Way follows what is so of itself.
26: The heavy is the root of the light; stillness is the lord of restlessness. Therefore the sage travels all day without leaving his baggage cart. Though there are splendid sights, he stays at ease above them. How can the lord of ten thousand chariots treat his own person lightly before the world? Light, and he loses the root; restless, and he loses his lordship.
27: A good traveler leaves no tracks; a good speaker makes no slips; a good counter needs no tallies; a good closer needs no bolt, yet what he shuts cannot be opened; a good binder needs no rope, yet what he ties cannot be undone. Therefore the sage is always good at saving people, so no one is cast away; always good at saving things, so nothing is cast away. This is called following the light. So the good man is the teacher of the not-good, and the not-good is the material of the good. Not to value one's teacher, not to love one's material, though clever, is to be greatly lost. This is called the essential mystery.
28: Know the male, keep to the female, and be the ravine of the world. Being the ravine of the world, constant virtue never leaves, and one returns to being an infant. Know the white, keep to the black, and be the model of the world. Being the model of the world, constant virtue never errs, and one returns to the limitless. Know glory, keep to disgrace, and be the valley of the world. Being the valley of the world, constant virtue is sufficient, and one returns to the uncarved block. When the uncarved block is split, it becomes vessels; the sage uses them and becomes head of the officials. So the great cutting does not cut.
29: One who wants to take the world and work on it, I see that he will not succeed. The world is a sacred vessel; it cannot be worked on. Whoever works on it ruins it; whoever grasps it loses it. So among things some lead and some follow, some breathe gently and some blow hard, some are strong and some weak, some break and some fall. Therefore the sage avoids the extreme, the extravagant, and the excessive.
30: One who assists a ruler with the Way does not use arms to force his will on the world; such deeds tend to rebound. Where armies have camped, thorns and brambles grow; after great wars, bad years are sure to follow. The good general achieves his aim and stops; he does not dare to use it to seize power. He achieves his aim but does not brag, achieves it but does not boast, achieves it but is not arrogant, achieves it because he had no choice, achieves it but does not force. Things in their prime grow old; this is called not following the Way, and what does not follow the Way soon ends.
31: Fine weapons are instruments of ill omen; things may detest them, so one who has the Way does not dwell with them. The gentleman at home honors the left; in war he honors the right. Weapons are instruments of ill omen, not the instruments of a gentleman; he uses them only when he has no choice, and calm restraint is best. Victory is not a thing to admire; to admire it is to delight in killing. One who delights in killing cannot have his way in the world. In happy affairs the left is honored; in sad affairs the right. The lieutenant general stands on the left, the commanding general on the right: that is, they are placed as at a funeral. When many people have been killed, mourn them with grief and tears; a victory in war is observed with funeral rites.
32: The Way is constant and nameless. The uncarved block, though small, no one in the world can make a subject of it. If lords and kings could keep to it, the ten thousand things would come as guests of their own accord. Heaven and earth unite and send down sweet dew; with no one ordering them, the people share it evenly by themselves. Once the uncarved is cut, there are names; once there are names, one should know when to stop; knowing when to stop, one can avoid danger. The Way in the world is like rivers and streams flowing to the rivers and the sea.
33: One who knows others is clever; one who knows himself is clear-sighted. One who conquers others has strength; one who conquers himself is strong. One who knows contentment is rich; one who acts with persistence has will. One who does not lose his place endures; one who dies but is not forgotten lives long.
34: The great Way flows everywhere; it can go left or right. The ten thousand things depend on it for life, and it does not turn them away; its work done, it claims no name; it clothes and nourishes the ten thousand things but does not act as their master. Ever without desire, it can be called small; the ten thousand things return to it, yet it does not act as their master, and it can be called great. Because to the end it never makes itself great, it can achieve greatness.
35: Hold to the great image and the world will come. It comes and meets no harm, but peace, calm, and ease. Music and food make passing travelers stop. But the Way, when spoken, is bland and has no flavor; looked at, it is not enough to see; listened to, it is not enough to hear; used, it cannot be used up.
36: What is to be shrunk must first be stretched; what is to be weakened must first be strengthened; what is to be abolished must first be raised up; what is to be taken must first be given. This is called subtle insight. The soft and weak overcome the hard and strong. Fish must not leave the deep; the sharp instruments of the state must not be shown to people.
37: The Way is constantly without contrivance, yet nothing is left undone. If lords and kings could keep to it, the ten thousand things would transform of themselves. If, transformed, they wish to stir, I will settle them with the nameless uncarved block. The nameless uncarved block brings freedom from desire. Without desire and so at rest, the world will settle of itself.
38: Superior virtue is not virtuous, and so it has virtue; inferior virtue never lets go of virtue, and so it has no virtue. Superior virtue does nothing and has no motive for doing; inferior virtue acts and has a motive for acting. Superior humaneness acts but has no motive; superior righteousness acts and has a motive; superior ritual acts, and when no one responds, it rolls up its sleeves and drags them along. So when the Way is lost there is virtue; when virtue is lost, humaneness; when humaneness is lost, righteousness; when righteousness is lost, ritual. Ritual is the thinning of loyalty and trust and the beginning of disorder. Foreknowledge is the flower of the Way and the beginning of folly. Therefore the great man dwells in the thick, not the thin; in the fruit, not the flower. So he rejects that and takes this.
39: Of old, these attained the One: heaven attained the One and became clear; earth attained the One and became steady; the spirits attained the One and became potent; the valley attained the One and became full; the ten thousand things attained the One and came to life; lords and kings attained the One and became the standard of the world. It is the One that brought this about. Were heaven not clear, it might split; were earth not steady, it might quake; were the spirits not potent, they might fade; were the valley not full, it might run dry; were the ten thousand things not alive, they might perish; were lords and kings not honored and high, they might fall. So the noble has the humble as its root, and the high has the low as its base. That is why lords and kings call themselves the orphan, the widower, the unworthy. Is this not taking the humble as root? Is it not? So count the parts of a carriage and there is no carriage. Do not wish to glitter like jade; be plain like stone.
40: Turning back is the movement of the Way; weakness is the use of the Way. The things of the world are born from being, and being is born from non-being.
41: When the best scholars hear of the Way, they practice it diligently. When middling scholars hear of the Way, they half keep it and half lose it. When the lowest scholars hear of the Way, they laugh out loud. If they did not laugh, it would not be the Way. So the established sayings have it: the bright Way seems dim; the Way forward seems to go back; the level Way seems rough; the highest virtue seems like a valley; the purest white seems soiled; ample virtue seems insufficient; firm virtue seems furtive; true substance seems to change; the great square has no corners; the great vessel is finished late; the great sound is faint; the great image has no shape. The Way is hidden and nameless. Only the Way is good at lending and at bringing to completion.
42: The Way gives birth to one, one gives birth to two, two gives birth to three, and three gives birth to the ten thousand things. The ten thousand things carry yin on their backs and embrace yang, and the blending of their breaths makes harmony. What people dislike is to be orphaned, widowed, or unworthy, yet kings and lords use these to name themselves. So things are sometimes increased by being diminished, and sometimes diminished by being increased. What others teach, I teach too: the violent do not die a natural death. I will take this as the father of my teaching.
43: The softest thing in the world gallops through the hardest. What has no substance enters where there is no gap. From this I know the benefit of doing without contrivance. The teaching without words and the benefit of doing without contrivance: few in the world attain them.
44: Your name or your life: which is dearer? Your life or your goods: which is worth more? Gain or loss: which is the harm? So excessive love must lead to great expense, and much hoarding must lead to heavy loss. Know contentment and you will not be disgraced; know when to stop and you will be in no danger; you can then last long.
45: Great perfection seems lacking, yet its use never wears out. Great fullness seems empty, yet its use is never exhausted. Great straightness seems bent; great skill seems clumsy; great eloquence seems tongue-tied. Restless movement overcomes cold; stillness overcomes heat. Clear stillness is the standard of the world.
46: When the world has the Way, galloping horses are turned back to haul manure. When the world lacks the Way, warhorses are bred on the borders. No disaster is greater than not knowing contentment; no fault is greater than the wish to acquire. So the contentment of knowing contentment is lasting contentment.
47: Without going out the door, one knows the world; without looking out the window, one sees the Way of heaven. The farther one goes, the less one knows. Therefore the sage knows without traveling, names things without seeing them, and accomplishes without acting.
48: In pursuing learning, one adds every day; in pursuing the Way, one sheds every day. Shed and shed again, until one reaches doing without contrivance; doing without contrivance, nothing is left undone. To win the world, always be free of meddling; once you meddle, you are not fit to win the world.
49: The sage has no fixed mind of his own; he takes the people's minds as his mind. Those who are good, I treat as good; those who are not good, I also treat as good; and so goodness is attained. Those who are trustworthy, I trust; those who are not trustworthy, I also trust; and so trust is attained. The sage in the world is cautious and withdrawn, and for the world's sake he muddles his mind. The people all fix their eyes and ears on him, and the sage treats them all as children.
50: Coming out into life, going in to death. Followers of life are three in ten; followers of death are three in ten; and those who live but by their own moves go to the place of death are also three in ten. Why is this? Because they cling too hard to life. I have heard that one good at preserving life travels on land without meeting rhinoceros or tiger, and goes into battle without wearing armor or carrying weapons. The rhinoceros finds nowhere to drive its horn, the tiger nowhere to set its claws, the weapon nowhere to lodge its blade. Why is this? Because he has no place of death.
51: The Way gives them life, virtue rears them, things give them shape, circumstances complete them. So the ten thousand things all honor the Way and prize virtue. The Way is honored and virtue prized not because anyone commands it, but always of their own accord. So the Way gives them life and virtue rears them; it raises them and nurtures them, settles them and matures them, feeds them and shelters them. It gives life but does not possess, acts but does not rely on it, raises but does not rule. This is called dark virtue.
52: The world has a beginning, which may be taken as the mother of the world. Having found the mother, one knows the children; knowing the children, one holds again to the mother, and to the end of life one is in no danger. Block the openings, shut the doors, and to the end of your life you will not be worn out. Open the openings, pursue your affairs, and to the end of your life you will not be saved. Seeing the small is called clarity; keeping to the soft is called strength. Use the light, return to clarity, and bring no harm upon yourself. This is called practicing the constant.
53: If I had even a little knowledge, walking on the great Way, I would fear only going astray. The great Way is very level, yet people love byways. The court is spotless, the fields are full of weeds, the granaries are empty; yet they wear embroidered clothes, carry sharp swords, are sated with food and drink, and have wealth to spare. This is called the boast of robbers. It is not the Way!
54: What is well planted cannot be uprooted; what is well held cannot slip away; and descendants will keep up the ancestral offerings without end. Cultivate it in yourself and your virtue will be genuine; cultivate it in your family and your virtue will be abundant; cultivate it in your village and your virtue will endure; cultivate it in your state and your virtue will flourish; cultivate it in the world and your virtue will be universal. So observe the self by the self, the family by the family, the village by the village, the state by the state, the world by the world. How do I know the world is so? By this.
55: One who holds virtue in its fullness is like a newborn child. Wasps, scorpions, and snakes do not sting him; wild beasts do not seize him; birds of prey do not strike him. His bones are weak and his sinews soft, yet his grip is firm. He does not yet know the union of male and female, yet he is fully aroused: this is the height of vitality. He cries all day without growing hoarse: this is the height of harmony. Knowing harmony is called the constant; knowing the constant is called clarity. Forcing life is called ill-omened; the mind driving the breath is called forcing. Things in their prime grow old; this is called not following the Way, and what does not follow the Way soon ends.
56: One who knows does not speak; one who speaks does not know. Block the openings, shut the doors, blunt the sharp, untie the tangled, soften the glare, mingle with the dust: this is called dark sameness. So one cannot get close to him, nor keep him at a distance; one cannot benefit him, nor harm him; one cannot ennoble him, nor debase him. So he is the most honored in the world.
57: Govern the state with rectitude, use troops with surprise, win the world by not meddling. How do I know it is so? By this. The more prohibitions in the world, the poorer the people; the more sharp tools among the people, the more the state is in confusion; the more skill and cunning people have, the more strange things appear; the more laws and orders are displayed, the more thieves and robbers there are. So the sage says: I do nothing, and the people transform themselves; I love stillness, and the people correct themselves; I do not meddle, and the people prosper themselves; I have no desires, and the people become simple themselves.
58: When government is dull and muddled, the people are honest and simple; when government is sharp and prying, the people are wanting. Misfortune is what good fortune leans on; good fortune is where misfortune hides. Who knows where it ends? There is no fixed rule. The correct turns again into the strange, the good turns again into the uncanny. People have been confused about this for a very long time. Therefore the sage is square but does not cut, sharp-edged but does not wound, straight but does not overreach, bright but does not dazzle.
59: In governing people and serving heaven, nothing is better than frugality. Only frugality means submitting early. Submitting early means accumulating virtue again and again. Accumulating virtue again and again, there is nothing one cannot overcome; when there is nothing one cannot overcome, no one knows one's limits; when no one knows one's limits, one can hold a state. Holding the mother of the state, one can last long. This is called the Way of deep roots and firm stems, of long life and lasting vision.
60: Governing a great state is like cooking a small fish. When the Way is used to oversee the world, ghosts lose their spirit power. It is not that the ghosts lose their power, but that their power does not harm people; it is not only that their power does not harm people, the sage also does not harm people. Since neither harms the other, their virtue flows back to the people together.
61: A great state is the lower reaches of a river, where the world meets, the female of the world. The female always overcomes the male by stillness, and by stillness takes the lower place. So a great state, by placing itself below a small state, wins the small state; a small state, by placing itself below a great state, wins over the great state. So one wins by taking the lower place, the other wins by being in the lower place. The great state wishes no more than to unite and shelter others; the small state wishes no more than to join and serve others. For both to get what they want, the great one should take the lower place.
62: The Way is the hidden refuge of the ten thousand things, the treasure of the good, and what keeps the not-good safe. Fine words can be sold in the market; honorable conduct can raise a person above others. Even if people are not good, why cast them away? So when the Son of Heaven is enthroned and the three ministers installed, though one presents a jade disc followed by a team of four horses, it is not as good as sitting still and offering this Way. Why did the ancients prize this Way? Did they not say that by it one who seeks shall find, and one who has offended shall be spared? So it is the most honored in the world.
63: Act without contrivance, work without meddling, taste the flavorless. Treat the small as great and the few as many; repay resentment with virtue. Plan the difficult while it is easy; do the great while it is small. The difficult things of the world must begin with the easy; the great things of the world must begin with the small. Therefore the sage never attempts the great, and so can achieve greatness. Light promises surely inspire little trust; taking much as easy surely brings much difficulty. Therefore even the sage treats things as difficult, and so in the end has no difficulty.
64: What is at rest is easy to hold; what has not yet shown signs is easy to plan for; what is brittle is easy to break; what is minute is easy to scatter. Deal with it before it exists; put it in order before disorder arises. A tree as wide as a man's embrace grows from a tiny shoot; a terrace of nine stories rises from a heap of earth; a journey of a thousand miles begins beneath one's feet. Whoever works on it ruins it; whoever grasps it loses it. Therefore the sage does not contrive and so does not fail; does not grasp and so does not lose. People in their undertakings often fail when they are on the verge of success. Be as careful at the end as at the beginning, and there will be no failure. Therefore the sage desires not to desire and does not prize goods hard to get; learns not to learn and brings people back from where they went too far. He helps the ten thousand things to be as they are of themselves and does not dare to contrive.
65: Those of old who were good at practicing the Way did not use it to make the people clever, but to keep them simple. The people are hard to govern because they have too much cunning. So governing a state by cunning is a curse to the state; not governing a state by cunning is a blessing to the state. Knowing these two is also knowing the pattern. Always knowing the pattern is called dark virtue. Dark virtue is deep, it is far-reaching; it turns back with things, and then attains great accord.
66: The rivers and the sea can be kings of the hundred valleys because they are good at staying below them; so they can be kings of the hundred valleys. Therefore one who wishes to be above the people must speak as if below them; one who wishes to lead the people must put himself behind them. So the sage is above, and the people do not feel his weight; he is in front, and the people do not feel harmed. So the world gladly pushes him forward and never tires of him. Because he does not contend, no one in the world can contend with him.
67: All the world says my Way is great but seems unlike anything. It is precisely because it is great that it seems unlike anything. Were it like something, it would long since have become petty. I have three treasures which I hold and keep: the first is compassion, the second is frugality, the third is not daring to be first in the world. Compassionate, one can be brave; frugal, one can be generous; not daring to be first in the world, one can become head of the officials. Now to be brave while forsaking compassion, generous while forsaking frugality, first while forsaking the last place: that is death! Compassion wins in battle and holds firm in defense. When heaven means to save someone, it guards him with compassion.
68: One good at being an officer is not warlike; one good at fighting does not get angry; one good at defeating the enemy does not engage; one good at using people places himself below them. This is called the virtue of not contending, the power of using people, matching heaven: the highest principle of old.
69: Those who use troops have a saying: I dare not play the host but play the guest; I dare not advance an inch but retreat a foot. This is called marching without ranks, rolling up sleeves without arms, dragging without an enemy, holding without weapons. No disaster is greater than taking the enemy lightly; taking the enemy lightly almost costs me my treasures. So when opposing armies meet, the side that grieves will win.
70: My words are very easy to understand and very easy to practice, yet no one in the world can understand them or practice them. Words have an ancestor; affairs have a master. It is only because people do not understand this that they do not understand me. Those who understand me are few, and so I am all the more prized. Therefore the sage wears coarse cloth and carries jade in his bosom.
71: To know that one does not know is best; not to know but think one knows is a sickness. Only by treating the sickness as sickness can one be free of it. The sage is free of the sickness because he treats the sickness as sickness; so he is free of it.
72: When the people do not fear authority, a great terror will come. Do not crowd their dwellings; do not oppress their livelihood. Only if they are not oppressed will they not grow weary. Therefore the sage knows himself but does not show himself; loves himself but does not exalt himself. So he rejects that and takes this.
73: Courage in daring leads to death; courage in not daring leads to life. Of these two, one benefits and one harms. What heaven hates, who knows why? Therefore even the sage treats it as difficult. The Way of heaven does not contend yet is good at winning, does not speak yet is good at answering, is not summoned yet comes of itself, is unhurried yet good at planning. Heaven's net is vast; its mesh is wide, yet nothing slips through.
74: If the people do not fear death, how can you frighten them with death? If the people always feared death, and those who did strange things I could seize and kill, who would dare? There is always an executioner who kills. To kill in place of the executioner is like cutting wood in place of the master carpenter. Of those who cut in place of the master carpenter, few avoid hurting their hands.
75: The people starve because those above them eat too much in taxes; that is why they starve. The people are hard to govern because those above them meddle; that is why they are hard to govern. The people take death lightly because they seek life too eagerly; that is why they take death lightly. Only those who do not strive for life are wiser than those who prize life.
76: When people are alive they are soft and weak; when they die they are hard and stiff. Plants and trees, when alive, are soft and tender; when they die, they are dry and withered. So the hard and stiff are followers of death; the soft and weak are followers of life. Therefore an army that is too strong will not win; a tree that is too strong will be cut down. The strong and great take the lower place; the soft and weak take the higher.
77: The Way of heaven, is it not like stretching a bow? The high end is pressed down, the low end is raised; what is in excess is reduced, what is lacking is supplied. The Way of heaven reduces excess and supplies what is lacking. The way of man is not so: it reduces the lacking to serve those who have excess. Who can take his excess to serve the world? Only one who has the Way. Therefore the sage acts but does not rely on it, completes the work but does not dwell in it; he does not wish to show his worth.
78: Nothing in the world is softer and weaker than water, yet for attacking the hard and strong nothing can surpass it, for nothing can take its place. That the weak overcomes the strong and the soft overcomes the hard, everyone in the world knows, yet no one can practice it. So the sage says: one who takes on the filth of the state is called the master of its altars; one who takes on the misfortunes of the state is the king of the world. True words seem contrary.
79: When a great resentment is reconciled, some resentment surely remains; how can that be counted good? Therefore the sage holds the left half of the tally and does not press others for payment. One who has virtue keeps to the tally; one without virtue keeps to collecting. The Way of heaven has no favorites; it is always with the good.
80: A small state with few people. Let there be tools for tens and hundreds of men, yet not used; let the people take death seriously and not move far away. Though they have boats and carriages, they have no occasion to ride them; though they have armor and weapons, they have no occasion to display them. Let people return to knotting cords and using them. Let them find their food sweet, their clothes fine, their homes peaceful, their customs a joy. Neighboring states may be in sight of one another, and the sounds of their roosters and dogs may be heard, yet the people grow old and die without ever going back and forth.
81: Trustworthy words are not beautiful; beautiful words are not trustworthy. The good do not argue; those who argue are not good. Those who know are not broad in learning; those broad in learning do not know. The sage does not hoard. The more he does for others, the more he has; the more he gives to others, the more he possesses. The Way of heaven benefits and does not harm; the Way of the sage acts and does not contend.
